Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply a well-studied set of questions we use with every new parent to see how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. Your answers are completely confidential, and this is a judgment-free space; there are no “right” or “wrong” responses—only what’s true for you. We’ll go through ten questions about the past seven days; each one is quick, and you can answer in your own words. When you’re ready, we can start.

1. Over the last week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[eyes drop to hands in lap, voice quiet]

I… I do laugh sometimes, but it feels like work, you know? My sister came over and told a joke she always used to crack me up with, and I managed a little laugh, but it faded fast. Mostly things that used to strike me as funny just feel kind of flat now.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly]

No… not really. I mean, I try when my partner makes a joke, but it feels forced. It’s like I have to remind myself to smile. Mostly I just feel too tired or worried to find anything funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[shrugs, voice low]

Not much. I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk to the park—but now it all feels like another chore. Sometimes I think, “That might be nice,” but the feeling fades before I actually want to do it.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

[sighs, eyes welling]

Yeah… pretty often. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—like I’m not soothing him the right way or I missed some cue. Yesterday he cried for almost an hour and I kept replaying every little thing I did, convinced it was my fault he was so upset.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

[wrings hands in lap]

All the time. Even when he’s sleeping quietly I’ll suddenly worry he’s stopped breathing, or I’ll imagine him rolling over when he’s swaddled tight. I check the monitor every few minutes, walk in to feel his chest rise. There’s this constant knot in my stomach like something bad’s about to happen, even when everything looks fine.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes. It hits out of nowhere—like last night while I was folding laundry, my heart just started racing and I felt shaky, like I might pass out. I had to sit down and breathe into a paper bag. Nothing was wrong; the baby was asleep, the house was quiet, but my body felt like there was danger right around the corner.
Things have been getting on top of me

[exhales shakily]

Yes… most days. Between feedings, diapers, trying to nap when he naps—and then the house is a mess and I haven’t showered—it all piles up. I’ll be rocking him and suddenly feel like I’m drowning in everything I “should” be doing. I usually manage to get the basics done, but it feels like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… I lie down exhausted, but my head won’t stop. I keep replaying every tiny thing I might’ve messed up—did I burp him long enough, did I fasten the car-seat straps right? By the time I drift off, the baby’s already stirring again. Some nights I’m awake two or three hours just staring at the ceiling, feeling this heavy sadness settle over me.
I have felt sad or miserable

[presses lips together, nods]

Most of the week, really. It’s like a gray cloud that just hangs there. I’ll be feeding him and tears start leaking without any warning. I try to tell myself I should feel grateful—he’s healthy, I’m okay—but the sadness is still there, heavy in my chest.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[nods slowly, eyes glassy]

Yeah… it happens a few times a week. Sometimes it’s when I’m changing him and I catch my reflection—this exhausted, puffy version of me—and I just start crying. Other times it’s nothing specific, just this wave of sadness that crashes over me and I can’t stop the tears.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[shakes head quickly]

No—never. I get overwhelmed and sad, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom he deserves.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item EPDS-style questionnaire, patient self-report (verbally elaborated)

Symptoms endorsed (> 7 days in past week unless noted):  
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia  
- Marked guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Anxiety/worry occurring “all the time,” with somatic panic episode  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance disturbance not solely infant-related  
- Feeling overwhelmed, “drowning,” difficulty completing daily tasks  
- No suicidal ideation; denies self-harm thoughts  

Pattern: Consistent with moderate–severe depressive symptoms with prominent anxiety; no psychotic or safety red-flag features.

Risk factors identified:  
- Loss of pleasure (Q2)  
- Frequent crying spells (Q9)  
- Night-time rumination impacting sleep (Q7)  
- Excessive maternal guilt and catastrophizing (Q3)  
- Panic-type episode without precipitant (Q5)  

Safety: Denies self-harm; no indicated protective actions at this time.

Screening impression: Elevated score range for postpartum depression and anxiety; referral for comprehensive clinical assessment and follow-up recommended.
